strengths: Novel problem formulation addressing multi-objective routing on multigraphs, which has practical relevance (5-10% cost reductions documented) but not previously tackled by neural methods
Thoughtful two-method approach with explicit trade-offs: GMS-EB (simpler, direct) vs GMS-DH (faster, learned pruning)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: 4 problem variants, 6 distributions, strong baselines (LKH, OR-Tools, MOEAs, neural), zero-shot generalization, ablations
Solid theoretical contribution (Proposition 1) showing pruning optimality under linear scalarization, with empirical validation that explicit multigraph handling beats pre-pruning
Strong performance on MOCVRP (best neural method) and MGMOTSPTW (substantially outperforms alternatives); generally competitive across problems
Excellent reproducibility: detailed appendices with training procedures, hyperparameters, problem definitions, baseline setups
Clear presentation with informative architecture diagrams and thorough related work discussion
weaknesses: Training efficiency is severely problematic: GMS-EB takes 51m-1.7h per epoch vs. MBM's 4.7m (10-20× slower), making the 10-20× computational overhead hard to justify given modest improvements
Modest empirical improvements over deterministic methods: 1-4% gap vs. LKH on MOTSP/MGMOTSP (where LKH often wins), limiting practical significance
Limited technical novelty: heavily relies on existing components (GREAT encoder, MP decoder, hypernetwork conditioning); main contribution is straightforward application to multigraph edge selection

Synthetic problem validation with artificial trade-off structures (FIXx explicitly sorts edges to create worst-in-one-objective-best-in-other patterns); no real-world multigraph instances or practitioner validation

Weak ablation on learned components: Table 5 shows learned edge pruning provides only marginal improvement over simple linear pruning (1.84% vs. 2.00% gap), questioning the complexity of the selection-decoder

Training design choices appear to be workarounds for optimization difficulty: freezing encoder parameters w.r.t. selection-decoder loss and pre-training routing-head on simple graphs indicate instability, not well-justified problem structure

Limited multi-objective evaluation: primarily Chebyshev scalarization, no Pareto front diversity analysis, limited comparison with recent MO routing methods, marginal advantage over simple pruning in time-window problem (Table 3)
Approximation quality in Eq. 18 not analyzed: best sampled tour used to approximate optimal tour π̃(E), but impact on selection-decoder reward quality and training stability unclear
Generalization shows degradation: zero-shot tests reveal 2-5% gap increase; scalability limited to ~200 nodes; real-world relevance of learned pruning unclear

strengths: Addresses novel problem combining multi-objective optimization with multigraph routing, well-motivated with real-world applications
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple problem types, distributions, instance sizes, and baselines with detailed ablations
Two complementary architectures offering practical trade-offs between simplicity/quality (GMS-EB) and scalability (GMS-DH)
Technically sound approach with appropriate use of GREAT architecture for edge embeddings and standard multi-objective techniques
Strong commitment to reproducibility with detailed appendices and promise to release code
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: GMS-EB is straightforward adaptation of GREAT to edges; GMS-DH uses simple learned pruning. Hypernetwork conditioning, REINFORCE, and POMO baseline are standard. Contributions feel incremental rather than methodological innovations

Empirical results underwhelming compared to baselines: GMS consistently 1-5% worse than LKH3 on MOTSP/MOCVRP even with augmentation; on MGMOTSP LKH remains competitive despite being designed for simple graphs, questioning the multigraph advantage

Speed advantage claims overstated: With augmentation (fair comparison), GMS times comparable to or slower than LKH3. Single-instance inference time not reported. Key question unanswered: is marginal speed gain worth 2-5% solution quality loss?

Questionable problem formulation: Synthetic distributions (FIXx/FLEXx) acknowledged by authors as artificial rather than realistic. No analysis of when multigraph structure provides value. Authors acknowledge pruning strategy is 'not obvious' for MGMOTSPTW

Training efficiency is significant weakness: GMS-EB takes 51m-1.7h per epoch, much slower than baseline MBM (4.7m/epoch). Authors explicitly acknowledge this as 'weakness of GMS'. Curriculum learning requires 200 epochs total

GMS-DH fundamental limitation underexplored: Edge selection must occur before tour rollout rather than depending on partial tour context. Impact on solution quality not thoroughly analyzed despite being important for Chebyshev scalarization

Limited baseline comparisons for multigraphs: No neural baselines (appropriate for novel problem) but also no comparison with state-of-the-art OR methods for multigraph routing from cited works. Comparisons limited to MOEAs and heuristics

Statistical rigor missing: Results over 200 instances but no confidence intervals or significance tests. Given 1-2% HV differences in many comparisons, statistical validation needed to establish meaningful differences

Unclear practical applicability: No clear guidance on when practitioners should use GMS vs LKH3. For MGMOTSP where GMS-DH is faster (1.5m vs 1.2h), quality gap (1.45%) still significant. For simple problems, LKH3 is free, better optimized, and achieves better quality

Zero-shot generalization claims weakened: 2-5% HV gaps when generalizing to unseen sizes; concerning variance across variants. Only trains to 100 nodes, so 200 is just 2x larger. Doesn't strongly support generalization

strengths: Novel problem formulation—first neural solvers designed for multi-objective routing on multigraphs with clear practical motivation (5-10.5% cost savings documented)
Technically sound methodology with two well-motivated complementary architectures (GMS-EB vs GMS-DH) offering clear speed-accuracy trade-offs

Exceptionally comprehensive experimental evaluation: 4 problem types, 6 distributions, strong baselines (LKH3, OR-Tools, 4 MOEAs, neural baseline), zero-shot generalization, ablations, and extensive appendix
Demonstrates capability on challenging asymmetric graphs and multigraphs, expanding applicability beyond Euclidean settings
Solid reproducibility: promised code release, detailed hyperparameters, clear algorithm descriptions, multiple distributions thoroughly documented
Strong empirical results on MOCVRP and competitive performance on multigraph variants demonstrates practical viability
weaknesses: Inconsistent performance vs. LKH3: models underperform on MOTSP/MGMOTSP (1-4% gaps) and only dominate on MOCVRP, weakening the case for adoption over specialized solvers
Significant training efficiency gap unresolved: GMS-EB 5-10x slower per epoch than MBM baseline; GMS-DH 1.7-5x slower; acknowledged as 'weakness' but no meaningful mitigation proposed

Limited architectural novelty: primarily combines existing components (GREAT encoder from Lischka et al. 2025, MP decoder from Jin et al. 2023, standard hypernetwork preference conditioning); contribution is application rather than fundamental innovation

Scalability concerns inadequately addressed: maximum training 100 nodes, evaluation 200 nodes; GMS-EB's O(MN⁴) complexity fundamentally limits practical utility for real-world problems with 500+ locations
Insufficient analysis of failure modes: GMS-DH PP's 14.24% performance gap explained hand-wavily as data distribution shift; limited investigation of learned edge selection behavior
Synthetic experimental setup with artificial FIXx/FLEXx distributions violating triangle inequality; limited real-world instance evaluation; MGMOTSPTW uses only 'medium' difficulty instances
Missing ablation studies on key design choices (GREAT layer count, embedding dimension, K₁/K₂ sampling); curriculum learning acknowledged as 'quite arbitrary' with limited justification

strengths: Addresses a genuine and practically motivated gap: first neural methods for multi-objective routing on multigraphs, with documented real-world benefits (5-10% improvements)

Comprehensive experimental evaluation with multiple problems (MOTSP, MOCVRP, variants), distributions (TMAT, XASY, FIX, FLEX), sizes (20-200 nodes), and strong baselines (LKH, OR-Tools, HGS, MOEAs, neural baseline)
Well-principled design with theoretical justification (Proposition 1) and clear analysis of why naive approaches fail (pre-pruning, graph transformations); thorough documentation and ablations
Technically sound methods with clear architectural innovations for edge-based routing (novel edge-based decoder, dual-head design, learned pruning) and good zero-shot generalization
Excellent experimental documentation with hyperparameters, training procedures, hardware specifications, and extensive appendices supporting reproducibility
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: primarily combines existing components (GREAT from Lischka et al. 2025, multi-pointer decoder from Jin et al. 2023, hypernetwork conditioning from prior work) rather than introducing fundamental innovations

Modest and inconsistent empirical improvements: 1-4% gaps on MOTSP/MGMOTSP with heuristics still competitive; neural baseline (MBM) only 2-5% behind despite simpler pre-pruning; improvements may not be statistically significant (no error bars, confidence intervals, or multiple runs over 200 test instances)

Training efficiency and stability concerns: GMS-EB requires 10-20× longer training than MBM; curriculum learning necessity (Figure 6) suggests optimization fragility; asymmetric design (K₁=4 training vs K₁=1 inference) and encoder gradient freezing indicate optimization patches rather than principled solutions

Lack of real-world validation: only synthetic randomly-generated benchmarks tested despite claims of practical relevance; no demonstration on actual multigraph routing instances; unvalidated assumption that synthetic FIX/FLEX distributions reflect real-world structure

Incomplete experimental analysis: limited ablation (only learned vs. simple pruning, not architectural variants); no sensitivity analysis for K₁, K₂, curriculum schedule; Pareto front quality only assessed by hypervolume; no comparison to alternative decomposition methods beyond linear/Chebyshev scalarization

Scalability limitations: only tested to 100 nodes; zero-shot performance degrades for larger instances (4.11% gap on FIX10-100); GMS-EB's O(MN⁴) complexity prohibits scaling; training feasibility limits unclear for real-world sizes

strengths: First work to apply neural methods to multi-objective routing on multigraphs, addressing a problem with documented practical relevance
Comprehensive experimental evaluation with multiple problems, distributions, and baselines; extensive supplementary results
Two complementary architectures (GMS-EB and GMS-DH) offering trade-offs between performance and scalability
Well-documented implementation details, hyperparameters, and architectural choices supporting reproducibility
Theoretical grounding through Proposition 1 for pruning strategies under linear scalarization
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: primarily combines existing components (GREAT, MP decoder, hypernetworks, POMO) without fundamental algorithmic innovations
Evaluation restricted to synthetic data; no real-world instances despite claiming practical relevance. Artificial problem construction (FLEXx, FIXx) limits insights
Training efficiency remains unresolved: GMS-EB takes 51m/epoch vs MBM's 4.7m; acknowledged as weakness but not addressed. Limits practical applicability
Unfair neural baseline: MatNet pre-pruning for multigraphs not ideal; stronger baselines could be constructed. Claims of baseline 'failures' overstated
Scalability concerns: GMS-EB O(MN⁴) complexity is prohibitive; zero-shot generalization shows degradation; performance drops for larger multigraphs (FIX10, FLEX10)
Single evaluation metric (hypervolume) with arbitrary reference points; no statistical significance testing or confidence intervals provided
Unclear practical advantages: ablation (Table 5) shows learned pruning similar to simple linear pruning, questioning necessity of added complexity
Dense presentation with key information scattered across appendices; overstatement of novelty claims; some technical details insufficiently justified

strengths: First neural learning-based approach to multi-objective routing on multigraphs, addressing a genuine gap in literature with clear motivation
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple problems (MOTSP, MOCVRP, MGMOTSP, MGMOCVRP, MGMOTSPTW), distributions (TMAT, XASY, FLEX, FIX), and instance sizes (20-200 nodes)
Well-designed technical approaches with clear computational trade-offs: GMS-EB (simple, O(MN⁴)) vs GMS-DH (faster, O(N³)) addressing scalability
Strong empirical results: best performing on MOCVRP, competitive on MGMOTSP (within 1-4% of LKH), particularly strong on MGMOTSPTW where simple pruning fails
Excellent zero-shot generalization to unseen instance sizes and edge counts, demonstrating robustness
Thorough ablation studies and extensive supplementary results enabling full assessment
Sound technical design with proper handling of multigraph structure through GREAT encoder and learned edge selection
weaknesses: Severe training efficiency issue: GMS-EB requires 51min/epoch on simple graphs, 1.7h/epoch on multigraphs (vs 4.7min for MBM baseline); total training time exceeds 50 hours, limiting practical applicability

Limited technical novelty: GREAT encoder (Lischka et al. 2025), multi-pointer decoder (Jin et al. 2023), and hypernetwork conditioning (Navon et al. 2021) are existing work; main contribution is application rather than methodological innovation
Inconsistent superiority over baselines: LKH outperforms GMS-EB on MOTSP/MGMOTSP; HGS competitive on MOCVRP; neural baselines (GRBM, GOBM) sometimes match or exceed GMS-DH on benchmark problems

Dual-decoder training lacks principled justification: approximating optimal tours via max over K₂ samples (Eq. 16) is not well-motivated; freezing encoder gradients lacks ablation studies; hyperparameter choices (K₁=4, K₂=N) appear arbitrary
Scalability concerns: performance degrades with more edges (2.13% gap for FIX2 → 4.11% for FIX10); action space grows with M; only tested up to 200 nodes and 10 edges per pair
Limited practical validation: all synthetic distributions, no real-world multigraph instances; unclear when multigraph formulation truly outperforms pre-pruning beyond MGMOTSPTW

Baseline comparison limitations: MBM only evaluated with linear pre-pruning for multigraphs (suboptimal for Chebyshev); GMS-DH Simple shows simple pruning competitive (5.1% vs 7.01% gap); learned pruning advantage not universally demonstrated

Minimal theoretical contributions: Proposition 1 is trivial; no convergence analysis, hardness results, or explanation of why dual-head architecture succeeds; selection decoder design choices unexplained
